title: Data in transit can be intercepted and used to identify parent
description: During parent registration, sensitive data (email, password, name, govt ID, six-digit code) is transmitted from ExternalEntity EE1 to Process P1. If intercepted, this data can be used to identify the parent user.

title: Data in transit can be disclosed to unauthorized parties
description: Registration data transmitted from EE1 to P1 may be exposed to unauthorized parties through network interception or man-in-the-middle attacks, leading to unauthorized disclosure of sensitive personal information.

title: Authentication Service can identify parent through stored registration data
description: Process P1 receives and stores sensitive registration data (email, password, name, govt ID, six-digit code), enabling identification of the parent user through this stored information.

title: Authentication Service may disclose stored registration data
description: Process P1 stores sensitive parent registration data and may disclose it to unauthorized parties through improper access controls, data breaches, or unauthorized sharing.

title: Authentication Service may collect excessive registration data
description: Process P1 collects multiple sensitive data elements (email, password, name, govt ID, six-digit code) during registration, potentially exceeding data minimization principles if not all fields are necessary for authentication.

title: Unauthorized Access to Stored Parent Account Data
description: Parent account data stored in MongoDB users collection may be accessed by unauthorized parties if access controls are insufficient. This represents an explicit disclosure risk where data is stored in a location that could be compromised.
assumptions: MongoDB collection has proper access controls and encryption at rest
uncertainty_note: Assuming standard MongoDB deployment without additional security hardening

title: Parent Account Data Interception in Transit
description: Parent account data transmitted from Authentication Service to MongoDB could be intercepted during transit if not properly encrypted. This flow carries personally identifiable information that could be used to link or identify individuals.
assumptions: Data is transmitted over network without end-to-end encryption
uncertainty_note: Assuming standard network transmission without TLS or similar encryption

title: Excessive Parent Account Data Collection
description: Authentication Service may be collecting more parent account data than strictly necessary for the authentication function, violating the minimality principle. This explicit disclosure occurs at the source when data is shared with the storage system.
assumptions: Data collection is not minimized to only what's required for authentication
uncertainty_note: Cannot verify if data collection is minimal without reviewing authentication service requirements

title: Identification via JWT token in transit
description: JWT tokens transmitted in the data flow contain user identifiers that can be used to identify the parent user to external observers or attackers intercepting the communication.

title: Linkability of user requests via JWT
description: The JWT token can be used to link multiple requests or data exchanges to the same parent user, enabling correlation of activities across different sessions or services.

title: Unauthorized disclosure of user data at destination
description: The parent user (external entity) may receive and process user data in ways that could lead to unauthorized disclosure, such as sharing with third parties or storing in insecure locations.

title: Usurpation via stolen JWT token
description: JWT tokens transmitted in transit could be intercepted and stolen, allowing an attacker to impersonate the parent user and gain unauthorized access to services.

title: Parent email used to link child account to parent identity
description: The parent email transmitted during child login can be used to link the child's account to the parent's identity, potentially revealing the parent-child relationship and enabling correlation of activities across systems.
assumptions: Parent email is unique and not anonymized; authentication service stores or logs this data.

title: Child's act of sharing parent credentials exposes identity
description: The child user's act of sharing parent email and password during login may expose the child's identity through the parent's email address, potentially revealing the child's relationship to the parent and their access to parent's account.
assumptions: Parent email is personally identifiable; child's login activity is logged or monitored.

title: Authentication service may disclose parent credentials to unauthorized parties
description: The authentication service receives and processes parent email and password, creating risk of disclosure if the service is compromised, improperly secured, or if credentials are logged/stored without adequate protection.
assumptions: Authentication service has access to credentials; service may log authentication attempts; service may have vulnerabilities.

title: Parent credentials intercepted during transmission
description: Parent email and password transmitted over the data flow could be intercepted by attackers, enabling unauthorized access to parent's account and potential misuse of credentials.
assumptions: Transmission may not be encrypted; network may be vulnerable to interception.

title: Identifiable data shared unnecessarily
description: The Authentication Service (P1) shares JWT tokens and child profiles with the Child User (EE2). These data elements contain personally identifiable information about the child that may be more detailed than necessary for the authentication purpose, creating a risk of over-disclosure.

title: Data in transit exposes identifying information
description: The JWT and child profiles transmitted in flow DF5 contain identifying information about the child user. If intercepted during transmission, this data could be used to identify the child to unauthorized parties.

title: Metadata enables linking of child to other systems
description: The JWT and child profiles may contain metadata (e.g., timestamps, device identifiers, or service-specific identifiers) that could be used to link the child's activities across different systems or services, potentially creating a comprehensive profile.

title: Child user may misuse JWT for impersonation
description: The Child User (EE2) receives JWT tokens that could potentially be misused to impersonate the child or gain unauthorized access to services, especially if the JWT is not properly secured or validated.

title: Linking via Government ID and Personal Attributes
description: The parent (EE1) shares child's government ID, name, DOB, and gender. This combination of attributes can be used to link this child's data to other records, databases, or external systems, potentially creating a comprehensive profile or enabling cross-referencing with other data sources.

title: Direct Identification via Government ID
description: The government ID is a direct identifier that can uniquely identify the child. Sharing this information at the source creates a risk that the child can be directly identified from the data shared, potentially exposing sensitive personal information.

title: Data in Transit Contains Linking Identifiers
description: The data flow itself contains government ID and other personal attributes that can be used to link this child's data to other records. Meta-data about the parties (e.g., who is creating the profile) combined with the data could enable identification or linking.

title: Unauthorized Data Disclosure at Destination
description: The Child Profile Management process (P3) receives sensitive personal data including government ID. If the process does not implement adequate access controls, encryption, or data protection measures, there is a risk of unauthorized disclosure of this sensitive information.

title: Usurpation/Impersonation Risk
description: With access to the child's government ID, name, DOB, and gender, an attacker could potentially impersonate the child in systems that use these attributes for authentication or verification, leading to unauthorized access or actions on behalf of the child.

title: Unintended Data Disclosure to Unauthorized Parties
description: Child profile data stored in MongoDB collection DS2 may be accessible to unauthorized personnel or systems, leading to disclosure of sensitive personal information about children.
assumptions: MongoDB collection lacks proper access controls or encryption at rest
uncertainty_note: Assuming standard MongoDB deployment without additional security hardening

title: Identification Risk During Data Transfer
description: Child profile data in transit between process P3 and data store DS2 may be intercepted or accessed, enabling identification of the child through the transferred personal data.
assumptions: Data flow lacks encryption or authentication mechanisms
uncertainty_note: Assuming data flow is not encrypted in transit

title: Linkability of Child Profile Data
description: Stored child profile data in DS2 may be linked with other data sources (e.g., parent information, medical records, school data) to create comprehensive profiles, increasing privacy risks.
assumptions: Data store may contain or be accessible to linked datasets
uncertainty_note: Depends on data governance and data linkage policies

title: Excessive Data Collection by Process
description: Process P3 may collect and store more child profile data than strictly necessary for the intended purpose, violating the minimality principle.
assumptions: Process collects data beyond what is required for child profile management
uncertainty_note: Depends on actual data collection practices and data model design

title: Unauthorized Modification of Child Profile
description: Stored child profile data in DS2 may be modified by unauthorized actors, leading to data integrity issues and potential harm to the child.
assumptions: Data store lacks proper access controls and audit mechanisms
uncertainty_note: Assuming standard MongoDB deployment without role-based access controls

title: Child Identifiability in Video Search and Comments
description: Child users share video search queries, likes, and comments that may contain personally identifiable information or context that could identify the child. Video content itself may reveal the child's identity, location, or activities.
assumptions: Child users may inadvertently share identifying information in video content or comments; video search queries may reveal personal interests or location.

title: Linkability of Video Metadata Across Services
description: Video metadata (timestamps, device info, IP addresses) transmitted in the data flow could be used to link the child's activity across different platforms or services, creating a comprehensive profile.
assumptions: Metadata is collected and transmitted with video data; metadata may be correlated with other data sources.

title: Non-compliance with Child Data Protection Regulations
description: Video Management Service may process child personal data without proper parental consent or in violation of COPPA/GDPR-K requirements. Improper data management of child information creates regulatory compliance risks.
assumptions: Child data requires special protection under regulations like COPPA and GDPR-K; consent mechanisms may be inadequate.

title: Unauthorized Disclosure of Video Content and Comments
description: Video content, search queries, likes, and comments stored by the Video Management Service may be disclosed to unauthorized parties through inadequate access controls, data breaches, or improper sharing with third parties.
assumptions: Video data is stored and may be accessed by multiple parties; access controls may be insufficient.

title: Child Account Impersonation and Usurpation
description: Child users may share credentials or video content that could be used by others to impersonate them, or their accounts may be compromised, leading to unauthorized actions under their identity.
assumptions: Child accounts may have weaker authentication; video content could be used to impersonate the child.

title: Identifying information in video metadata
description: Video metadata (timestamps, locations, device IDs, etc.) can contain identifying information that may be used to identify individuals associated with the video content.
assumptions: Metadata fields may include personally identifiable information or quasi-identifiers that can be combined to identify individuals.
uncertainty_note: Using I.1.2 from context as it directly addresses metadata with identified information

title: Unauthorized access to stored video data
description: MongoDB collection may be accessible to unauthorized parties, leading to disclosure of stored video files and metadata containing personal information.
assumptions: DataStore may not have adequate access controls or encryption at rest.
uncertainty_note: Dd.1.1 is a standard data disclosure node; severity depends on MongoDB security configuration

title: Linkability of video records across time and context
description: Video metadata can be used to link multiple video records to the same individual or activity, potentially revealing patterns of behavior or associations.
assumptions: Metadata contains consistent identifiers (e.g., user IDs, device IDs, timestamps) that can be correlated across different video records.
uncertainty_note: L.1.1 is a standard linkability node; applicability depends on metadata schema

title: Unintended Data Disclosure via Child Profile Storage
description: Storing child search and watch history in MongoDB creates a data disclosure risk. This personal data about children's online behavior is stored persistently, potentially exceeding minimality requirements if not strictly necessary for the service functionality.
assumptions: The stored history may contain personally identifiable information or be linkable to identify the child
uncertainty_note: Using Dd.1.1 as it represents explicit disclosure by design; uncertainty about whether this is avoidable given service requirements

title: Linkability of Child Search/Watch History
description: Search and watch history data may be linkable across sessions or with other data sources, enabling profiling of the child's interests, preferences, and behavior patterns over time.
assumptions: The stored history can be correlated with other data to build a comprehensive profile
uncertainty_note: Assuming the data contains sufficient identifying characteristics for linkage

title: Identification Risk from Stored Child Activity Data
description: Child search and watch history may contain or be combined with information that can identify the child, especially if the data includes timestamps, device information, or other metadata.
assumptions: The data or its metadata can be used to identify the child
uncertainty_note: Depends on what specific data fields are stored and whether they contain direct identifiers

title: Unauthorized Access to Child Profile Data
description: The MongoDB childprofiles collection may be accessible by unauthorized parties, leading to unauthorized access to sensitive child activity data.
assumptions: The data store lacks adequate access controls or encryption
uncertainty_note: Assuming standard MongoDB deployment without specific security measures mentioned

title: Excessive Data Collection at Source
description: Process P3 may collect and share more child data than strictly necessary for the intended functionality, violating the minimality principle.
assumptions: The system collects search and watch history when it may not be essential for core service delivery
uncertainty_note: Cannot determine if this data is truly necessary for the service without more context

title: User video content contains personally identifiable information
description: The parent user uploading video may inadvertently include personally identifiable information (PII) such as faces, voices, or contextual details that could identify them or others in the video.

title: Video metadata enables user linking
description: Metadata accompanying the video upload (timestamps, device IDs, IP addresses, user IDs) could be used to link video content to specific users or correlate with other data sources.

title: Video data interception during transmission
description: Video data in transit could be intercepted by unauthorized parties if the transmission channel lacks adequate encryption or security controls.

title: Video Management Service unauthorized data sharing
description: The Video Management Service may share, store, or process the uploaded video data with third parties without proper user consent or legal basis.

title: Non-compliant video data retention and processing
description: The Video Management Service may retain or process video data in ways that violate applicable privacy regulations (e.g., GDPR, CCPA) regarding consent, purpose limitation, or data minimization.

title: Video data repurposing beyond original intent
description: The Video Management Service may use the uploaded video data for purposes beyond the original upload intent (e.g., training AI models, analytics, marketing) without user consent.

title: Video stream metadata enables child identification
description: Metadata accompanying the video stream (e.g., timestamps, device identifiers, IP addresses) could be used to identify the child user or link them to other data flows, compromising their anonymity during transmission.

title: Video content enables cross-referencing and linking
description: The video content itself may contain visual or contextual information that allows linking the child to other data sources, such as location data, family information, or other personal records.

title: Unauthorized access to child's video data at destination
description: The child user (EE2) may not have adequate security controls to protect the received video data, leading to unauthorized access, viewing, or sharing of the video content by third parties.

title: Non-compliant video data handling for minors
description: The Video Management Service (P2) may not comply with data protection regulations (e.g., GDPR, COPPA) regarding the collection, transmission, and processing of video data involving minors, creating legal and privacy compliance risks.

title: Explicit disclosure of child browsing data to AI engine
description: Child browsing data is explicitly transferred from MongoDB collection to AI Recommendation Engine, constituting an explicit disclosure of personal data. This disclosure may violate the minimality principle if the data is not strictly necessary for the AI's function.
assumptions: The AI engine processes and potentially stores the child data.

title: Identification of children through browsing data
description: The AI Recommendation Engine may use child browsing data to identify individual children, potentially creating profiles or linking browsing behavior to specific identities.
assumptions: The AI engine has access to identifying information or can infer identities from browsing patterns.

title: Unauthorized interception of child data in transit
description: Child browsing data transmitted from MongoDB to AI engine may be intercepted by unauthorized parties during transit, especially if the connection is not properly secured.
assumptions: The data transmission may not be adequately encrypted or protected.

title: Non-compliance with child data protection regulations
description: The transfer and processing of child browsing data may violate regulations such as COPPA (Children's Online Privacy Protection Act) or GDPR-K (children's data under GDPR), which impose strict requirements for collecting and processing children's personal data.
assumptions: The system may not have proper consent mechanisms or data minimization controls for children.
uncertainty_note: Regulatory requirements may vary by jurisdiction; this is a general assessment.

title: Explicit Disclosure of Browsing Data to Third-Party Advertisers
description: The AI Recommendation Engine (P4) intentionally shares browsing data with third-party advertisers (EE3) as part of its planned data flow. This represents an explicit data disclosure where personal data is transferred across a system boundary to a known third party. The minimality principle is at risk as the scope of browsing data shared may exceed what is strictly necessary for the advertising purpose.

title: Linkability of Browsing Data via Metadata
description: Data in transit (DF14) may contain metadata or contextual information that allows third parties to link browsing patterns to specific individuals or devices. This linkability threat arises from the data-centric nature of the flow, where metadata about the parties involved could be used to identify or correlate users across different data sources.

title: Uncontrolled Data Processing by Advertisers
description: Third-party advertisers (EE3) receive browsing data and may process, store, or share it in ways that extend beyond the original intended purpose. The destination element's handling of the data creates a data disclosure risk as advertisers may use the data for profiling, cross-referencing with other data sources, or further distribution without adequate privacy safeguards.

title: Identification Risk During Data Transfer
description: Browsing data transmitted in the flow (DF14) may contain personally identifiable information or quasi-identifiers that could be used to identify individuals. The data in transit is vulnerable to identification if intercepted or if the data format allows direct or indirect identification of users.

title: Child data sharing enables profile linking
description: The Child Profile Management process shares child history data with the parent user, which could enable linking of this child's information with other data sources (e.g., school records, medical records, other family members) to build a comprehensive profile of the child beyond what was intended.

title: Child identifiable information disclosed to parent
description: The process shares child history data that may contain personally identifiable information about the child, potentially revealing sensitive details about the child's development, health, or behavior that were not intended for broad access.

title: Metadata in data flow enables linking
description: Metadata accompanying the child history data in transit (e.g., timestamps, access patterns, or identifiers) could be used to link this data with other data flows or systems, potentially revealing associations between the child and other entities.

title: Parent user may disclose child data to unauthorized parties
description: The parent user, upon receiving the child history data, may share or disclose this sensitive information to third parties (e.g., other family members, friends, or online platforms) without proper authorization, leading to unauthorized access to the child's personal information.

title: Parent user may misuse child data for impersonation
description: The parent user could potentially use the child's personal information from the history data to impersonate the child in other systems or contexts, or to gain unauthorized access to child-related services.
